strengths: The paper poses an interesting challenge in terms of using LLMs and large corpora of unstructured text to aid the process of constructing causal graphical models.
The authors attempt a quantitative evaluation.

The authors put a good deal of work into testing their algorithm. They took sets of variables from the epidemiology literature, and recruited 3 experts to compare gold standard causal graphs to compare their output to.
Much of the exposition about how the algorithm worked was admirably clear, with a couple of glaring exceptions.
They put effort into showing that each part of the hybrid algorithm contributed to the overall result.
The results that they reported are limited, but given the cost of creating gold standard graphs, understandable.
The results showed that their hybrid algorithm did outperform competitors.
The paper addresses an important problem, showing potential by integrating various existing techniques.
It includes extensive experimental evaluations of causal discovery using publicly available data, showcasing how the potential of the proposed framework.
An iterative approach for causal discovery allows to stop whenever a sufficiently stable solution is found, lowering the computational complexity.
Automated data collection can be useful to bootstrap the causal discovery procedure.
Missing variables proposal is an interesting approach to causal insufficiency that should be investigated more.
weaknesses: The evaluation of IRIS focuses more on replicating human expectations than on accurately estimating causal effects, and the ground truth based on human judges eliminates any possible mismatch between the graphical model formalism and actual causal effects in the world.

The authors appear to show that the method improves accuracy, but not why it improves accuracy; a mechanism is not clearly described or proven by detailed experiments, making the results unconvincing.
The authors describe the construction of cyclic models but do not clearly define the semantics of those models, leaving it unclear what their cyclic models mean in a formal sense.
The authors do not define a semantics of temporal causal models and do not mention challenges such as hierarchical dependence or aggregation.

The authors incorrectly claim to relax the causal sufficiency assumption because IRIS proposes new variables; in reality, IRIS's ability to propose additional variables does not relax the assumption and the paper lacks evidence that the added variables correspond to latent confounders.
The authors do not provide evidence that the discovered variables satisfy necessary assumptions of causal graphical models, such as modularity (autonomy) or independence of causal mechanisms.

The authors do not appear to effectively address key challenges of extracting structured data from text, such as variation in unit definitions, heterogeneity of data collection conditions, and biased sampling, and they do not discuss these threats to validity or how they are mitigated.
It is unclear how the collection of data from documents is even possible; the authors should make clearer what numeric data appears in documents and how it can be effectively extracted.
One writing issue interferes with effective reading of the paper: the authors provide citations without parentheses, making it difficult to separate citations from ordinary text.
The authors gave evidence that IRIS improved the construction of causal graphs compared to previous LLM algorithms, but it is unclear from the paper why that is.

It is unclear whether the value extraction always forces the output to be binary; the prompt makes it sound that way, yet the article applies value extraction to variables with three values, and the meaning of precision and recall for this multiclass case is not explained.

The value extraction was applied to the AppleGastrome data set, but the paper lacks a detailed explanation of what the AppleGastrome documents look like, requiring the reader to consult the original paper.

Value extraction appears to produce only binary (True/False) entries, discarding information from variables that can have many values, which may impair the causal discovery algorithms that expect richer data.
Causal discovery algorithms assume i.i.d. data, but the documents used for value extraction may be dependent (e.g., through citation), violating this assumption.
Selecting documents based on term queries may introduce selection bias, further affecting the validity of the causal discovery results.
In the example applications of IRIS, very few confounders were found among the new variables, suggesting that the observed accuracy may not generalize to other settings.
The integration of new variables into the causal graph is handled naively; it is unclear how to reconcile conflicts between background knowledge and edge orientations when new variables are added.
Applicability of causal discovery methods is questionable because the value‑extraction data is aggregated from documents and represents co‑occurrence rather than true causal relationships.

The paper overlooks the assumptions of causal discovery methods (acyclicity, causal sufficiency) and provides no evidence that the results satisfy these assumptions, calling into question the causal interpretation.

Experimental results show that causal discovery methods alone do not work effectively here; the highest‑performing methods include Verified Causal Relations (VCR), indicating that pre‑verified causal knowledge is critical.
Methods reported in Tables 3‑7 vary inconsistently across datasets, which is scientifically unsound to selectively report results.
Concluding that IRIS outperforms other methods based on one variation performing better than comparison methods in a single dataset introduces potential bias due to multiple comparisons.
The data collection and value extraction is performed by querying large databases with coarse queries based on iterative keyword reduction, which may limit data quality.

The statistical causal discovery in the paper computes relationships based on term‑document frequency, which does not correspond to the literature that computes statistical properties from actual data about the variables of interest.
There is no guarantee that the LLMs are not trained on the same papers used to evaluate the datasets, so the generalization and validity of the proposed approach cannot be concluded.
